title: JESUS KNEW JUDAS WOULD BETRAY HIM. SO WHY DID HE LET HIM STAY?
paragraphs: JESUS KNEW JUDAS WOULD BETRAY HIM. SO WHY DID HE LET HIM STAY?

He knew who would sell Him. He knew the price. He knew the kiss was coming. Yet Jesus still washed Judas’ feet, shared His table, and allowed him to remain among the Twelve. The reason is more heartbreaking—and more revealing about the heart of Christ—than most people realize.
There is something deeply unsettling about the story of Judas Iscariot.
Not simply that a man betrayed Jesus for thirty pieces of silver.
Not simply that someone who witnessed miracles, heard the greatest Teacher who ever lived, and walked beside the Son of God could eventually hand Him over to His enemies.
It is something even more disturbing.
Jesus knew.
Before the betrayal.
Before the secret negotiations.
Before the silver changed hands.
Before Judas entered the garden with armed men.
Jesus already knew what was living inside the heart of the man sitting at His table.
And still, He let Judas stay.
Think about that for a moment.

If you knew someone close to you would eventually destroy your reputation, expose you to your enemies, and participate in a plot that would cost you your life, would you continue inviting that person into your home?
Would you share your food?
Would you let that person travel with you, listen to your private conversations, and remain among your closest companions?
Most of us would begin creating distance the moment we discovered the truth.
We would protect ourselves.
We would close the door.
We might even tell everyone what that person was planning.
But Jesus did something that confronts nearly everything we understand about betrayal, patience, love, and divine mercy.
He allowed Judas to remain close enough to betray Him.
And if we misunderstand why, we may misunderstand something essential about the Gospel itself.
Because the story of Judas is not merely about a traitor who sold Jesus.
It is also about the terrifying possibility of being physically close to Christ while remaining spiritually far from Him.
And it raises a question that should make every believer examine their own heart:
What if the most dangerous place to be is not outside the church, but inside it—close enough to know the language of faith, yet unwilling to surrender to the Lord of faith?
The Gospel of John gives us an extraordinary detail.
Jesus said:
“Have not I chosen you twelve, and one of you is a devil?” (John 6:70, KJV).
John immediately explains that Jesus was speaking about Judas Iscariot, the one who would betray Him.
This was not a sudden discovery on the night of the Last Supper.
John 6:64 tells us that Jesus knew from the beginning who did not believe and who would betray Him.
The Greek text says:
ᾔδει γὰρ ἐξ ἀρχῆς ὁ Ἰησοῦς
Ēdei gar ex archēs ho Iēsous.
“For Jesus knew from the beginning.”

The phrase ex archēs means “from the beginning.” In this context, it emphasizes that Judas’ unbelief and future betrayal were not hidden from Jesus. It does not require us to assume that every event in Judas’ life had already been described in detail to the other disciples.
Jesus was not deceived into choosing Judas.
He was not blindsided by a trusted companion.
He did not discover the betrayal when Judas finally walked into Gethsemane.
He knew.
But knowing that Judas would betray Him did not mean Jesus Himself caused Judas to become a betrayer.
That distinction matters.
God's foreknowledge does not make Him the author of human evil. Scripture holds Judas accountable for his actions even while showing that Christ's suffering fulfilled God's redemptive purpose.
In Acts 2:23, Peter declares that Jesus was delivered up according to God's determined counsel and foreknowledge, yet those responsible for crucifying Him remained morally accountable.
Divine sovereignty did not turn human wickedness into innocence.
And God's ability to accomplish redemption through betrayal did not make betrayal righteous.
This is where the story begins to become painfully personal.
Because many of us have quietly asked God questions we are almost ashamed to speak aloud.
“Lord, if You knew that person would hurt me, why did You allow them into my life?”
“If You knew that friendship would end in betrayal, why did You let me trust them?”
“If You knew that relationship would break my heart, why didn't You stop it before it began?”
Those questions are real.
And the story of Judas does not give us permission to pretend that every betrayal has a simple explanation.

It certainly does not mean Christians should knowingly remain in abusive or dangerous relationships. Jesus' voluntary journey toward the cross was a unique act of redemption, not a command for victims to abandon healthy boundaries or personal safety.
But it does reveal something astonishing.
Jesus was never helpless before the betrayal that would lead Him to the cross.
He willingly moved toward the suffering He had come to bear.
In John 10:18, Jesus says of His life:
“No man taketh it from me, but I lay it down of myself.”
Judas would betray Him.
Religious leaders would condemn Him.
Roman authorities would crucify Him.
Yet none of these events meant that Jesus had lost control of His mission.
The cross was not an emergency solution to a plan that had gone wrong.
It was central to the saving purpose of God.
And Judas, despite his wicked intentions, could not overturn that purpose.
But here is where the story becomes almost unbearable.
Jesus did not merely tolerate Judas from a distance.
He gave him a place among the Twelve.
Judas traveled with the disciples.
He heard Jesus teach about forgiveness, hypocrisy, repentance, the kingdom of God, and the danger of loving money.
He witnessed the ministry of the One whom he would eventually betray.
He was even entrusted with the group's moneybag.
John 12:6 tells us that Judas was a thief who used to take what was put into it.
Consider the contradiction.
The man entrusted with the money was secretly stealing.
The man traveling with the Truth was living a lie.
The man who heard Jesus warn against serving both God and money was allowing greed to occupy his heart.
And somehow, outward religious participation continued.
That should disturb us.
Because Judas did not begin his public life as a man standing outside the circle of discipleship shouting against Jesus.
He was inside.
He belonged to the visible company of the Twelve.
He could speak the language.
He knew the routines.
He had access to the ministry.
And when Jesus announced that one of them would betray Him, the disciples did not immediately point to Judas.
They began questioning who it could be.
A person can become so familiar with the activities of Christianity that everyone assumes their heart belongs to Christ.
But familiarity is not the same as faith.
Ministry is not the same as surrender.
Religious responsibility is not the same as spiritual transformation.
You can carry a Bible and still refuse its authority.
You can sing about the cross and still resist the One who died upon it.
You can defend Christian truth in public while secretly protecting sin in private.
And this is why the story of Judas must never become an opportunity for us to feel superior to him.
It should drive us toward honest self-examination.
Not because every struggling Christian is secretly Judas.
Not because every temptation proves someone has never truly believed.
But because the human heart is capable of astonishing self-deception.
The question is not merely whether we have spent time around Jesus.
The question is whether we have truly come to Him in repentance and faith.
And then comes one of the most emotionally powerful scenes in all of Scripture.
The night before the crucifixion.
A room.
A meal.
Twelve disciples.
And Jesus, knowing that His hour had come, rose from supper.
He laid aside His outer garments.
He took a towel.
He poured water into a basin.
And He began washing the disciples' feet.
Try to picture the room.
The Lord of glory kneeling before ordinary men.
The hands that had touched lepers now touching dusty feet.
The One through whom all things were made taking the position of a servant.
And Judas was there.
John 13:2 tells us that the devil had already put betrayal into Judas' heart. John then describes Jesus washing the disciples' feet before identifying Judas as the betrayer later in the chapter.

The natural reading is that Judas was present for the foot washing and was included in this astonishing act of humility, although John does not narrate a separate moment in which Jesus specifically washes Judas' feet.
That distinction is worth preserving.
We do not need to invent details to make Scripture powerful.
What John actually tells us is already overwhelming.
Jesus knew what was coming.
And Jesus served.
He did not stop being the perfect Servant because a betrayer was present.
He did not abandon His character because someone else had abandoned faithfulness.
His humility was not dependent upon the worthiness of the people around Him.
This does not mean Jesus approved of Judas' betrayal.
It means the coming betrayal did not change who Jesus was.
And perhaps that is one of the most beautiful truths hidden in this terrible night.
The sinfulness of the people around Jesus never made Jesus less holy, less truthful, or less faithful to the Father's will.
But we must be careful here.
The foot washing was not merely a sentimental gesture.
Jesus was teaching His disciples the nature of humble service and the cleansing they needed from Him.
When Peter resisted, Jesus answered:
“If I wash thee not, thou hast no part with me.” (John 13:8, KJV).
And then Jesus said something chilling:
“Ye are clean, but not all.” (John 13:10, KJV).
John explains that Jesus said this because He knew who would betray Him.
In other words, a man could be present while Jesus washed feet and still remain spiritually unclean.
Physical proximity did not guarantee inward cleansing.
Participation in a sacred moment did not automatically produce saving faith.
And this is where the story reaches beyond Judas and into our own lives.
There are people who know how to look devoted while privately drifting away.
People who still attend worship but have stopped praying honestly.
People who serve in ministry while carrying secret bitterness.
People who can encourage everyone else while slowly losing their own hunger for God.
Some are fighting sin and desperately longing to return.
Others have learned to protect sin while maintaining a religious appearance.
Those are not the same spiritual condition.
And Jesus knows the difference.
He does not despise the broken believer who comes confessing sin.
First John 1:9 assures us that God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse those who confess their sins.
But Scripture also warns against hardening our hearts through the deceitfulness of sin (Hebrews 3:13).
The danger is not that a wounded Christian struggles.
The danger is learning to live comfortably with rebellion while refusing the mercy that calls us to repent.
Judas heard the warnings.
He saw the example.
He remained among the disciples.
Yet Scripture never portrays him as a repentant follower who entrusted himself to Christ for salvation.
And the darkness continued growing.
Then came the moment when betrayal took a definite price.
Matthew 26:14–16 records Judas approaching the chief priests and asking what they would give him to deliver Jesus into their hands.
They weighed out thirty pieces of silver.
Thirty pieces.
The exact purchasing power of that payment is difficult to translate into modern currency, and the Gospels do not specify the precise denomination of each coin.
But the spiritual horror does not depend on calculating its modern value.
Judas was willing to hand over his Master for money.
The tragedy was not that Jesus had suddenly become worth only thirty pieces of silver.
The tragedy was that Judas was willing to betray the priceless Son of God for something that could be counted.
And isn't that how sin often works?
It offers something measurable in exchange for something immeasurably precious.
A moment of pleasure in exchange for faithfulness.
A dishonest advantage in exchange for integrity.
A secret indulgence in exchange for a clear conscience.
A temporary reward in exchange for obedience to God.
Not every sinful compromise is equivalent to Judas' betrayal.
But the warning is unmistakable.
When we begin treating Christ as negotiable, we are walking into dangerous territory.
And still, Jesus moved toward the cross.
At the Last Supper, He announced that one of those eating with Him would betray Him.
Matthew 26:24 records His solemn warning:
“The Son of man goeth as it is written of him: but woe unto that man by whom the Son of man is betrayed!”
Do not miss the tension.
Jesus said His suffering would unfold as Scripture had foretold.
And in the same breath, He declared judgment upon the betrayer.
The betrayal was known.
The betrayal was wicked.
The betrayer was responsible.
Jesus' foreknowledge did not remove Judas' guilt.
And the fulfillment of Scripture did not excuse his choices.
In John 13:18, Jesus also invokes Psalm 41:9:
“He that eateth bread with me hath lifted up his heel against me.”
The Hebrew of Psalm 41:9 includes the expression:
הִגְדִּיל עָלַי עָקֵב
Higdil ʿalay ʿaqev.
Literally, the imagery concerns someone magnifying or raising a heel against another.
The language communicates treachery by someone once trusted.
In its original setting, Psalm 41 describes the pain of betrayal by a close companion. Jesus applies this Scripture to the betrayal He is about to experience.
This matters because the Bible does not treat betrayal as an insignificant inconvenience.
It recognizes the wound.
The pain of betrayal is not simply that an enemy opposed you.
It is that someone close enough to share your table became an instrument of harm.
Someone who knew your voice.
Someone who had seen your kindness.
Someone who had been welcomed into your confidence.
And perhaps that is why betrayal can hurt so deeply.
It attacks not only what happened, but what you believed was true about the relationship.
If you have ever been betrayed, you may know that peculiar grief.
You replay conversations.
You remember moments that once seemed genuine.
You wonder which smiles were sincere.
You begin questioning whether your own trust was foolish.
And sometimes the wound follows you into relationships with people who never harmed you.
But the Gospel gives us a Savior who is not unfamiliar with betrayal.
Hebrews 4:15 teaches that Jesus is able to sympathize with our weaknesses, having been tempted in every respect as we are, yet without sin.
He knows what it is to be rejected.
He knows what it is to be abandoned.
He knows what it is to be betrayed by someone who shared His table.
And He remained without sin.
That means you can bring your wounded heart to Him without having to explain why betrayal hurts.
He knows.
But there is another question we cannot avoid.
If Jesus knew Judas would betray Him, why didn't He remove him before the betrayal happened?
Scripture does not give us a private conversation in which Jesus explains every reason for allowing Judas to remain.
We should not pretend to know what God has not revealed.
But Scripture does reveal enough to understand several essential truths.
Jesus' choice of the Twelve was made with full knowledge of Judas' future betrayal.
Jesus' death fulfilled the saving purpose of God.
The betrayal fulfilled Scripture without making Judas innocent.
And Jesus' continued ministry among the disciples revealed the consistency of His own righteousness, humility, and obedience.
Most importantly, Judas' betrayal did not create the Gospel.
Jesus' sacrificial death and victorious resurrection are the heart of the Gospel.
Judas was not the hero of redemption.
His sin was not a virtue.
And Christians should never praise betrayal as though wickedness were necessary goodness.
Rather, we worship a God so sovereign and holy that human evil cannot defeat His saving purpose.
What Judas intended for betrayal, God incorporated into the events through which Christ would accomplish redemption.
That does not make God the author of Judas' greed.
It makes the triumph of Christ all the more astonishing.
But the story does not end at the table.
It moves into the darkness of Gethsemane.
Judas arrives with a crowd carrying swords and clubs.
And he has arranged a sign.
A kiss.
The ordinary gesture of greeting and affection becomes the signal of betrayal.
Matthew 26:49 records Judas approaching Jesus, greeting Him as Rabbi, and kissing Him.
Then Jesus says:
“Friend, wherefore art thou come?” (Matthew 26:50, KJV).
The Greek word translated “Friend” here is:
ἑταῖρε
Hetaire.
It is a form of address that can mean “companion,” “comrade,” or “friend,” depending on context.
It is not the same word as philos, the familiar Greek term often associated with personal affection.
That matters because we should not build an entire doctrine on the assumption that Jesus was expressing intimate friendship through this particular word.
Yet the scene remains extraordinary.
Jesus does not respond with uncontrolled rage.
He does not pretend the betrayal is harmless.
In Luke 22:48, He confronts Judas directly:
“Judas, betrayest thou the Son of man with a kiss?”
There is a terrible contrast in that question.
A kiss should communicate affection.
Judas used it to conceal treachery.
An outward expression of closeness became the instrument of surrendering Jesus to His enemies.
And the question almost seems to echo through the centuries.
How often do people offer God the outward signs of devotion while withholding their hearts?
How often do we speak lovingly about Jesus while resisting His commands?
How often do we want the reputation of being Christian without the surrender that following Christ requires?
This is not a call to become suspicious of every believer.
It is a call to stop confusing religious performance with genuine discipleship.
Jesus is not looking for a flawless performance.
He calls sinners to repent and believe the Gospel.
He calls the weary to come to Him.
He calls the broken to receive His mercy.
But He also calls us to follow Him.
And following Him means we cannot make peace with the very sin He came to save us from.
Then comes another devastating part of Judas' story.
After Jesus was condemned, Matthew 27:3 says Judas experienced remorse and returned the thirty pieces of silver.
The Greek verb used is:
μεταμεληθείς
Metamelētheis.
It conveys regret, remorse, or a change of feeling.
The New Testament also uses the word metanoia for repentance, a turning of mind and life toward God.
We should not oversimplify these words as though one always means false sorrow and the other always means genuine salvation. Their meanings can overlap depending on context.
But Matthew's account shows Judas' remorse ending in despair and death rather than describing a return to Jesus in trusting repentance.
Judas confessed that he had betrayed innocent blood.
He returned the money.
Yet he did not find the restoration that the Gospel later shows so powerfully in Peter.
And here is the comparison that should break our hearts.
Judas betrayed Jesus.
Peter denied Jesus.
Judas handed Jesus over to His enemies.
Peter publicly insisted that he did not know Him.
Both men sinned grievously.
Both experienced the crushing reality of what they had done.
But their stories moved in different directions.
Judas' story ends in tragedy.
Peter wept bitterly, and after the resurrection Jesus restored him.
In John 21, the risen Christ questioned Peter three times about his love and entrusted him with the care of His sheep.
Peter's restoration was not because his sin had been small.
His denial was serious.
His restoration testified to the grace of the risen Savior.
And this contrast brings us to one of the most important truths in the entire story.
Your greatest hope is not that you have never failed Jesus. Your greatest hope is that Jesus saves sinners who turn to Him.
The answer to sin is not hiding.
It is not religious acting.
It is not trying to purchase forgiveness through good works.
It is repentance and faith in the crucified and risen Christ.
Second Corinthians 7:10 speaks of godly sorrow producing repentance leading to salvation, while worldly sorrow produces death.
The difference is not merely how intensely someone feels guilty.
The question is where that sorrow leads.
Does it drive us into hopelessness?
Or does it bring us honestly before the mercy of God?
Maybe you are reading this with something hidden in your life.
A habit nobody knows about.
A compromise you keep promising to abandon.
A prayer life that has quietly disappeared.
A relationship with God that looks healthy to everyone else but feels frighteningly distant to you.
Perhaps you still post Bible verses.
Perhaps you still attend church.
Perhaps you still encourage others.
But deep inside, you know there is something you have refused to surrender.
Please hear this carefully.
Do not confuse the patience of God with His approval of your sin.
Second Peter 3:9 teaches that the Lord is patient, not wishing that any should perish but that all should reach repentance.
His patience is not permission to remain in rebellion.
It is a reason to turn to Him while the call to repentance is before you.
And do not allow the story of Judas to convince you that your sin has placed you beyond the reach of Christ's mercy.
Judas' story is a warning.
It is not a declaration that every person who has failed terribly must share his end.
Jesus says in John 6:37:
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.”
That is a promise worth holding onto.
If you come to Christ, you are not approaching a Savior who reluctantly tolerates repentant sinners.
You are coming to the One who gave Himself for sinners.
The One who carried our sins in His body on the tree.
The One who shed His blood for the forgiveness of sins.
The One who rose again and lives forever.
And perhaps you need to hear this tonight:
You do not have to keep pretending.
You do not have to polish your spiritual appearance before coming to Jesus.
You do not have to wait until your life looks impressive.
Come honestly.
Confess what is wrong.
Turn away from what is destroying you.
Trust the Savior who died and rose again.
Because the Gospel is not the announcement that good people finally earned their way into God's presence.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
And that changes everything.
Someone reading silently may need to know that repentance, forgiveness, and a new beginning are real.
Because the story of Judas does not simply ask us to look backward at one man's betrayal.
It asks us to look inward.
And then upward.
Toward the Savior who was betrayed, condemned, crucified, buried, and raised in victory.
The cross tells us that our sin is more serious than we want to admit.
But it also tells us that God's grace in Jesus Christ is greater than we could ever deserve.
At Calvary, Jesus did not excuse sin.
He bore sin.
He did not declare evil harmless.
He suffered to redeem sinners from its guilt and power.
He did not come merely to improve our religious appearance.
He came to reconcile us to God.
And that is why this story belongs to the Gospel rather than merely to the history of betrayal.
Judas shows us the tragedy of remaining close to holy things without surrendering to the Holy One. Jesus shows us the mercy of God reaching toward sinners through the cross.
One warns us.
The Other saves us.
And the invitation remains open to everyone who hears His voice and comes to Him in faith.
This is also why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to entertain people with religious stories that disappear from memory by tomorrow.
Not to build a community that confuses emotional reactions with spiritual transformation.
But to keep placing the truth of Scripture before real people facing real battles.
People struggling with temptation.
People rebuilding their faith.
People carrying wounds from betrayal.
People who have been away from God for years.
People who need more than another inspirational sentence.
They need the Word of God.
They need the Gospel of Jesus Christ.
They need encouragement that leads toward obedience, repentance, forgiveness, and genuine discipleship.
And if these messages have helped you understand Scripture, confront sin, or find courage to return to Christ, I want to invite you to help us continue.
But let us be biblically clear.
It does not purchase His favor.
It does not replace your responsibility to care for your family, give faithfully according to your convictions, or support your local church.
And it should not be confused with a mandatory biblical tithe.
Second Corinthians 9:7 teaches that giving should not be done reluctantly or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
We want support that flows from love for Christ and a genuine desire to help others grow in Him—not guilt, fear, or pressure.
These products can serve as reminders of biblical truth, personal discipleship tools, or meaningful gifts for people you love.
It is participating in the work of making Christ known.
We want the Word of God to remain accessible to people who are hungry for truth, including those who cannot afford to give financially.
Your prayers matter.
Your encouragement matters.
Your willingness to share biblical truth matters.
Think of the friend who quietly stopped attending church.
The brother who is losing hope.
The sister who has been wounded by betrayal.
The parent praying for a wandering child.
The person who appears strong but is secretly struggling with sin.
Someone in your circle may need to hear that Jesus knows the truth about the human heart—and still calls sinners to come to Him.
Because we do not want people merely to read about Jesus.
We want people to know Him.
To repent.
To believe.
To grow.
To endure.
To experience the transforming grace of God.
And now, before you leave this story, return with me to that upper room one final time.
Jesus is at the table.
The disciples are gathered.
Judas is still there.
The cross is approaching.
Jesus knows the betrayal is coming.
And He continues toward the Father's will.
Not because Judas is stronger than Him.
Not because the darkness has won.
Not because God has lost control.
But because Jesus has come to accomplish a redemption no betrayal can defeat.
In a matter of hours, Judas will hand Him over.
The disciples will scatter.
Peter will deny Him.
Jesus will be condemned.
And the One who never sinned will bear the sins of many.
But three days after His burial, the tomb will be empty.
Death will not hold Him.
The betrayal will not have the final word.
The cross will not be the end.
Jesus Christ will rise.
And the risen Savior will continue calling sinners out of darkness into His marvelous light.
So perhaps the most important question tonight is not simply why Jesus allowed Judas to stay among the Twelve.
Perhaps it is this:
Now that you know Jesus sees the truth about your heart, what will you do with His call to repentance and faith?
Will you continue hiding behind appearances?
Will you keep negotiating with the sin that is pulling you away from Him?
Or will you come honestly to the One who gave His life to save sinners?
You cannot rewrite yesterday.
You cannot undo every failure.
You cannot return to the moments before your worst decisions.
But through Jesus Christ, forgiveness is real.
Redemption is real.
A transformed life is possible.
And your past does not have to be the final chapter of your story.
Judas stood close enough to kiss the face of Jesus and still walked into darkness. Today, don't settle for being close to the things of Christ when Christ Himself is calling you to come home.
